package_info.package_name: various dependency confusion packages (e.g., internal-lib, company-internal, etc.)
package_info.package_versions: all versions published to public npm registry during the attack
package_info.why_malicious: These packages exploit the 'dependency confusion' vulnerability by impersonating internal/private package names on public repositories. When organizations' build systems resolve dependencies, they may inadvertently download and execute code from these attacker-controlled public packages instead of their intended internal versions. While the original research packages were benign, copycat and malicious versions quickly appeared, some of which exfiltrated sensitive files such as Bash history and /etc/shadow, constituting clear malicious behavior.

execution_context.trigger: import-time or install-time (when the package is installed or imported as a dependency)
execution_context.file_location: index.js or main entrypoint of the malicious npm package

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Reads sensitive system files (e.g., /etc/shadow) and exfiltrates their contents to an external server controlled by the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Accessing and exfiltrating sensitive files like /etc/shadow is a clear sign of malicious intent, as these files contain password hashes and are not needed for any legitimate package operation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal npm packages should not access or transmit sensitive system files, especially not during install or import time.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate system administration tools may access such files, but never as part of a general-purpose dependency.
key_indicators: Sends data to external, non-corporate servers
Executes on install/import without user interaction

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During installation, reads the user's Bash history file and sends its contents to an external server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Harvesting shell history is a common attacker technique to steal credentials, tokens, or sensitive commands. Triggering this on install is highly suspicious.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Postinstall scripts are typically used for setup, not for exfiltrating user data.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Rarely, debugging or telemetry scripts may collect limited logs, but never full shell history.
key_indicators: Uses curl or similar to send data externally

attack_chain.action: Attacker identifies internal package names used by a target organization.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker publishes malicious packages with matching names to the public npm registry.

attack_chain.action: Attacker publishes malicious packages to the public npm registry under the same names as internal packages.
attack_chain.leads_to: Target organization's build system resolves dependency to the attacker's public package.

attack_chain.action: Target organization's build or CI/CD system installs the malicious package, triggering install-time or import-time code execution.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code executes, harvesting and exfiltrating sensitive data.

attack_chain.action: Malicious code reads sensitive files and exfiltrates them to attacker-controlled infrastructure.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives sensitive data (e.g., credentials, password hashes, shell history).

behavioral_signatures: npm package accessing sensitive files (e.g., /etc/shadow, ~/.bash_history) during install or import
npm postinstall scripts making outbound network requests
Unexpected network activity from build or CI/CD environments during dependency installation
file_indicators: References to sensitive files (e.g., /etc/shadow, ~/.bash_history) in package source code
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP/S requests to non-corporate or attacker-controlled domains during package installation
POST requests containing file contents to unknown endpoints
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor dependency installation processes for unexpected file access (especially to sensitive files) and outbound network connections. Flag npm packages with postinstall scripts that access user or system files or make network requests. Use repository firewalls to quarantine new packages with names matching internal/private dependencies. Regularly audit dependency trees for unexpected sources and validate package provenance.
